title: A Design Leader Who Never Stopped Building
subtitle: Prototypes that run against real APIs, a quality bar the build enforces, and research that has changed a product's direction

cv.label: Download CV (PDF)
cv.note: Tailored for the Head of Product Design role

bio.short: I lead design functions and I still build. I prototype in real code against real production APIs, and engineering ships from that code. The quality bar lives in the build rather than in the review.
bio.long:
I lead design functions and I still build. At Ninox I ran design and, for four months, product as well. Nine people across design, UX writing, product management and data science. I hired two, promoted two, and coached a design lead through a relationship with engineering that was going badly. The last year has been deliberately hands-on. At Bibel TV I own UI quality across iOS, Android, web and connected TV. I prototype in real code against real production APIs rather than in specs, and engineering ships from that code. The part I would bring to a consumer product is where I put the quality bar. Not in review — in the build. Six checks run identically on a laptop and in CI, and they refuse work that has left the system. Two were written against mistakes I watched an AI assistant make: a token reference that does not resolve, and a color hardcoded into a component. Neither shows up as a visual difference, so the build is the only place they surface.

The color engine is the craft half of the same instinct. K-means clustering in OKLCH rather than RGB, so artwork-driven themes carry even perceptual weight across a grid. WCAG contrast validated inside the algorithm, so nothing ships failing it. At ChurchDesk a booking capability cut coordination time by 70% with 90% acceptance. And research has changed a company's direction: at Spreadshirt leadership wanted a 60-second automated journey. Interviews with shop owners found that the design step was the part they valued most, and the strategy moved.

context.emphasis: Hands-on first, because the posting says 'highly hands-on' in its opening line and 'ready to dive into the details' in its closing one. Then craft as something implemented rather than asserted, then coaching a team, then the data-driven habit. Spreadshirt is the consumer evidence and it is a strong one, so it carries the third clause of the subtitle and leads the browseable set.
